parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a training company to book a place on a first-aid course.
script: Good morning, Riverside Training, Callum speaking. How can I help?
Hello. I'd like to sign up for one of your first-aid courses, please. I saw the details in the community newsletter.
Certainly. We run a few different ones. Is it for work, or more of a general course?

It's for a volunteer role, actually. I coach an under-12s football team on Saturday mornings, and the club has just told all the coaches that we need a first-aid certificate by the end of the season. I'll admit my mother has been unwell lately, so it will be useful at home as well, but the club is the real reason.
Right, that makes sense. Then the one-day Emergency First Aid course is what you want. Some people choose the two-day course, but for coaches the one-day is enough. Can I take some details?
Thanks, I've got that. And is there a number I can reach you on?
07700 900 418. Lovely. Now, the next course is on Saturday the 7th of March, but I'm afraid that one's full. The one after that is on 14 March, and there are still a few places.
Saturday is ideal, because I work during the week. What time does it start? The newsletter said half past nine.
Ah, that was the old timetable, I'm afraid. We've moved it earlier so that everyone can finish by half past four. It starts at 9.15, and you need to arrive a few minutes before that to sign in.
OK, 9.15. And where is it held?

At the moment we're running the Saturday courses in a room at Harcourt Library, on Mill Street. It's about five minutes from the station. We used to use the community centre, but that's closed for repairs.
Oh, that's handy. I walk past the library anyway. How much does it cost?
The standard fee is 95 pounds. However, if you live in the borough, there's a reduced rate, which is 85 pounds. Do you live locally?
Yes, I'm in Elm Park, so that should count.
Then it's 85. That includes the manual and the certificate.
Is there anywhere to park nearby, just in case I decide to drive?

There's a small car park behind the library, but it fills up early on Saturdays, so I'd come on foot or by bus if you can. It's free after midday, though I'm afraid that won't help you in the morning.

No, I'm afraid not. There's a cafe round the corner, but the break is only forty minutes, so most people bring a packed lunch. I'd suggest you do the same. And wear something comfortable, because you'll be practising on the floor.
That's fine. Does the certificate last for life, or do I have to renew it? I think someone told me it was only valid for a year.
No, it's valid for three years. After that you'd need to do a half-day refresher course, but you won't have to take the whole thing again.
Good, that's longer than I thought. And how do I pay?
There are a few options. You can give me your card number over the phone now, or you can pay online using the link in your confirmation email, or you can bring a cheque on the day.
I'd rather not give my card details over the phone, and I always forget to bring cheques. I'll use the link, if that's all right.
That's absolutely fine. Just make sure you do it within three days, or we'll have to offer your place to someone on the waiting list.
I'll do it this evening. Thank you very much for your help, Callum.
You're welcome, Joanna. We'll see you on the 14th. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A ranger welcomes visitors at the start of a walk round a wildlife reserve.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Saltmarsh Wildlife Reserve. My name's Dale, and I'm one of the rangers here. Before we set off on the walk, I'd like to tell you a little about the reserve and explain what's available and where, so that you can make the most of your day.

First, some background. A lot of people assume that the reserve was set up by the council. The council does own the car park, but the marsh itself was bought in 1996 by a group of local residents who were worried that it was going to be drained and turned into farmland. They raised the money themselves, and they still manage the site today with the help of our volunteers.

Most visitors come for the birds. In summer we do get some lovely orchids along the sea wall, and I know a few of you will have come for those, but the real star of the show is the huge flocks of wading birds that arrive from the Arctic every winter. Some days there are tens of thousands of them on the mudflats, and when they all take off together it's quite something.

A few practical points. An adult ticket costs 7 pounds, and children under five come in free, although everyone else pays a reduced price. The thing I'd like you to remember is that your ticket is valid for a whole year. If you get it stamped at the visitor centre desk on your way out, you can come back as often as you like until the same date next year, so it's very good value if you live nearby.

Now, a word about dogs. I know many of you would love to bring them, but they're not allowed on the marsh paths, because they disturb the nesting birds, even when they're on a lead. What you can do is take them along the woodland trail, as long as they stay on a lead the whole time.

And one safety point. The sea path is lovely, but the tide here comes in faster than you'd expect, and parts of the path can be cut off. Please don't rely on guesswork. Check the tide times on the board outside the visitor centre before you set off. You don't need to register with us, and while boots are a good idea in wet weather, you'll be fine in ordinary shoes today.

Right, let me tell you what you'll find as we walk round. We're standing at the visitor centre. Inside there's the information desk, where you can borrow binoculars free of charge. They're very popular, so I'd suggest you pick up a pair now if you haven't brought your own.

Just across the courtyard is the Kingfisher Cafe. It serves hot meals and homemade cakes, and it's also a good place to buy presents, because it sells crafts made by local artists, such as pottery and woven baskets. There's no Wi-Fi, I'm afraid, so you'll have to enjoy the view instead.

Behind the cafe you'll see a large wooden building, which we call the Education Barn. It's mainly used by school groups during the week, but at weekends it's open to everyone, and what most families enjoy is the pond-dipping. We provide the nets and the trays, so there's nothing for you to bring.

From there, a short path takes you to the Reedbed Hide. It's the best place to see the marsh harriers, and at weekends there are volunteers on hand who give short talks about the birds, at eleven and again at two o'clock. Do remember to keep your voices down inside, as the birds are easily startled.

Finally, the Woodland Trail, which starts at the far end of the car park. It's about a mile long, and the surface is firm and flat all the way round, so it's suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. The marsh paths, by contrast, can be muddy and uneven.
That's everything from me for now. If you have any questions, just ask. Otherwise, shall we make a start?

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students plan a questionnaire about public transport for a course project.
script: Hi, Owen. Sorry I'm late. Have you been waiting long?
Not really. I've just been reading the assignment brief again. We have to hand in a draft of the questionnaire by Friday, so I thought we should settle the design today.
Right. And we're definitely going with the bus service topic?

Yes. Dr Hughes said we could choose anything related to transport, but I think this will be the most interesting. The council cut the number 14 route to campus last term, so we all know someone who's been affected.
True. My flatmate has to leave an hour earlier now. I did think about suggesting cycling, but nobody would care about that as much as the bus cuts.
Exactly. So, how are we going to reach people? I'd thought of standing at the bus station with clipboards.

Hmm, but people there are always rushing to catch something, and it'd be freezing in November. And we'd only get people who still use the buses, whereas we want students who've stopped using them too.
Fair point. What about handing the forms out at the end of lectures?
We'd need permission from every lecturer, and it would take ages. I think the easiest thing is to send it out by email through the student union. They've already said they'd forward it to everyone.
OK, that's a much better idea. It would give us a bigger sample, too.
Now, length. We have to keep it short. If it takes ten minutes, nobody will finish it.
I'd say three minutes at the most.
Three is a bit optimistic if we want some open questions as well. Let's say five minutes and about fifteen questions.
Five it is. And before we send it out, we ought to try it on a few people.
A pilot, yes. Will Dr Hughes check it for us?

I did ask, but she said she doesn't have time to approve it. She'll only look at the final version. So I'll ask my housemates and a few people from my seminar group to complete it and tell us what's confusing.
Good. And what about personal details? Should we ask for names?

I don't think so. People will be less honest if they think we can identify them, and it means we won't need the data protection forms. We can just ask which faculty they're in and what year they're in.
Agreed. No names. Shall we look at your draft questions now? I've read through them and made a few notes.
The first one: 'Do you agree that buses are far too expensive?' I'd change that. It pushes people towards answering yes. We need something neutral.
Oh, I see. So how about 'How would you rate the cost of bus fares?'

Much better. Then number two: 'How often and why do you use the bus?' That's really two questions in one. Someone might go every day for one reason and only occasionally for another, so we should separate them.
OK. Number three: 'How do you feel about public transport?'
That's too broad, isn't it? People could write about trains, taxis, anything. We should say which service we mean and which aspect, whether it's reliability, comfort or whatever.
Right. Number four: 'What is your household income?' I wanted to see whether students with less money rely on buses more.
I see why, but I think a lot of people would be reluctant to answer that, and it might make them stop filling it in. Why don't we ask whether they have a part-time job instead?
Fine. Number five is about how they get to campus: 'Do you come by bus or by car?'
The problem there is that there are only two choices. Lots of students walk or cycle or get a lift. We need to add more options, otherwise they'll have to pick an answer that isn't true.
Got it. The last one is the satisfaction scale from one to five.
That one's fine as it is. It'll be easy to analyse.
Great. I'll redo the draft tonight and send it to you tomorrow morning.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the ecosystem of the Arctic tundra.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to look at the ecosystem of the Arctic tundra, one of the coldest and, in some ways, least understood habitats on Earth.

Let's start with the word itself. 'Tundra' comes to us through Russian, from a Sami word meaning a treeless plain. So the first thing to know is that the tundra is defined by what it lacks. It lies north of the tree line, and it covers roughly a tenth of the planet's land surface. Even in July the temperature rarely rises much above ten degrees, and the winters are long and dark.

Surprisingly, the tundra is also very dry. Many people expect such an icy place to receive a great deal of snow, but annual precipitation is generally less than 250 millimetres, which is about the same as many deserts. Some textbooks give a figure of 350, but that applies to the southern fringe, where the tundra merges into the forest. The cold air simply can't hold much moisture.

The feature that shapes everything else is permafrost, which is ground that stays frozen all year round, sometimes to a depth of hundreds of metres. In summer, only the top layer, known as the active layer, thaws. In the forests to the south this might be two metres deep, but in the tundra it's only about 50 centimetres. Because water can't drain downwards through the frozen ground, the surface turns into a mass of pools and bogs, which is why the tundra becomes so marshy in summer.

Now let's think about the plants. With such a thin layer of thawed soil, trees can't put down roots, and the growing season lasts only about sixty days. The vegetation consists of mosses, grasses, lichens and dwarf shrubs such as the Arctic willow. These plants have two important adaptations. The first is that they grow very low to the ground, which helps them avoid the wind, because the wind strips away moisture and snaps tall stems. The second is that many have leaves with a hairy surface, which traps a layer of warm air next to the plant.

Turning to the animals, the caribou, or reindeer as they're known in Europe, travel hundreds of kilometres between their summer and winter feeding grounds. Their winter diet consists mainly of lichens, which they find under the snow by smell and dig out with their hooves.

The best-known small animal is the lemming, whose numbers rise and fall in a regular cycle. It was once thought that the cycle repeated every three years, but better data from long-term studies show that the peak comes round every 4 years. The cycle matters because the predators depend on it. When lemming numbers collapse, Arctic foxes and snowy owls go hungry, and many of them fail to breed.

Another remarkable survivor is the musk ox. It has long outer hair over a layer of soft underwool called qiviut, which is about 8 times warmer than the wool of a sheep. The animals stand together in a circle when wolves approach, with the calves in the middle, and the thick coats make them almost impossible to attack.

Although the summer is short, it's a time of abundance. Billions of mosquitoes and midges hatch out of the pools. That sounds unpleasant, and it is, but they provide food for the millions of migratory birds that fly thousands of kilometres to breed here. People sometimes suggest that the birds come for the seeds, or even for the mild weather, but it's really the insects that draw them.

Finally, let's consider the threats. The tundra is warming much faster than the global average. As the permafrost thaws, plant material that has been frozen for thousands of years begins to rot, and it releases gases. Carbon dioxide is certainly one of them, and it gets most of the attention, but the greater worry is methane, which traps heat far more effectively. Some scientists fear that this could create a feedback loop, in which warming releases more gas, which in turn causes more warming.
I'll say more about that next week. For now, are there any questions about the basic structure of the ecosystem?

passages.title: The machine that changed the wardrobe
paras: A  For most of human history, every item of clothing was sewn by hand. A plain linen shirt could take a skilled worker the best part of a day, and a tailored coat several days, which is why ordinary families owned only a few garments and mended them again and again. The idea of speeding up the work with a machine occurred to inventors long before anyone managed to build one that functioned. In 1790 an English cabinet-maker named Thomas Saint was granted a patent for a device that would pierce leather and pull a thread through it, but there is no evidence that he ever completed a working model, and his design lay forgotten for decades.

B  The first machine to be used in earnest was the work of a French tailor, Barthélemy Thimonnier, who patented his design in 1830. It used a hooked needle to form a simple chain stitch, and within a few years he had set up a workshop in Paris with some eighty machines, stitching uniforms for the army. The venture did not last. According to a story repeated for generations, a crowd of tailors who feared for their livelihoods broke into the workshop and smashed the machines, and Thimonnier barely escaped. Historians now suspect that the tale has been embellished, but it captures a fear that would follow the sewing machine wherever it went. Chain stitch also had a practical weakness: pull one end of the thread and the whole seam unravelled.

C  The problem of the weak seam was solved in America. Elias Howe, a mechanic from Massachusetts, patented a machine in 1846 that used two threads, one carried by a needle with the eye near its point and the other by a shuttle beneath the fabric. The two threads locked together, producing a lockstitch that was strong enough for clothing. Howe, however, found it hard to attract buyers at home. He spent several years in England trying to sell the idea, and returned to find that others were manufacturing machines that borrowed heavily from his design.

D  Chief among those others was Isaac Singer, a former actor and engineer who in 1851 patented a machine of his own. Singer's version was not a radical new invention; its real strength lay in practical improvements. The needle moved up and down rather than sideways, the fabric was held flat on a table by a presser foot, and a foot-operated treadle left the operator's hands free to guide the cloth. Howe went to court, and won, and Singer was obliged to pay him a royalty on every machine sold. By 1856 the quarrels had become so costly that the main manufacturers agreed to pool their patents and license them to one another, an arrangement that allowed the industry to grow without constant litigation.

E  Singer's greatest innovation, though, may have been commercial rather than mechanical. A machine cost more than most families earned in several months, so he began to offer hire purchase: customers paid a small deposit and then settled the balance in monthly instalments. He also opened showrooms, where women demonstrated the machines, and hired agents to teach buyers how to use them. Within a decade his company was selling more machines than any rival, and the practice of buying expensive goods on credit, which Singer helped to popularise, was later adopted for everything from pianos to cars.

F  The effects on the clothing trade were dramatic. Factories could now produce shirts, coats and trousers in quantities that no workshop of hand-sewers could match, and they could do so in standard sizes, so that garments could be sold ready to wear rather than made to measure. Prices fell and, for the first time, working people could afford more than one set of clothes. Military demand accelerated the change: during the American Civil War, armies needed uniforms by the hundred thousand, and manufacturers who could meet such orders became wealthy. Tailors did not disappear, but many were reduced to alterations and repairs, or were employed by the factories themselves.

G  The social consequences were less happy. Because the machines were light and cheap to run, much of the stitching was handed out to people working at home or in cramped workshops, usually for a payment for each piece completed. Most of these workers were women, many of them recent immigrants, and they often worked for twelve or fourteen hours a day for very low pay. These crowded workshops, which became known as sweatshops, were a target for reformers, and the dreadful conditions eventually helped to produce the laws on factory safety and working hours that were passed in the early twentieth century.

H  At the same time, the sewing machine brought some women a degree of independence. In ordinary households it shortened the time spent on making and mending clothes, and a woman with a machine could take in sewing for neighbours and earn money without leaving home. Advertisements presented it as a means for a wife to help with the family income, and even as a path to running her own dressmaking business. Historians continue to debate whether the machine freed women from drudgery or simply created new kinds of labour, but few doubt that it altered everyday life more than almost any other domestic device of its century.

passages.title: Cities on the line
paras: A  When the first passenger railways opened in the 1830s, few people foresaw how profoundly they would reshape the places they served. Before then, a town's size was limited by how far food and fuel could be carried by cart, canal or coastal ship, and most people lived within walking distance of their work. The railway abolished those limits. Within a single generation it determined which towns would flourish, which would stagnate, and what form every large city would take.

B  Some places owed their very existence to the railway. Swindon was a modest market town until a railway company chose it as the site for its repair works in the 1840s; Crewe was little more than a crossing in the farmland before the same thing happened there. The companies built houses, schools and even a hospital for their employees, and the towns grew in the pattern of the factory rather than the market. Even small villages could be transformed. A farming community that gained a station might see its produce reach city markets within hours, and a fishing port could send fresh fish inland on the day of the catch, so that for the first time the diets of inland towns began to include fresh sea fish. Elsewhere, the railways acted as a funnel. Chicago, which sat at the junction of lines from the prairies to the west and the markets of the east, became the place where grain was stored, cattle were slaughtered and timber was sorted, and its population multiplied several times in the second half of the century.

C  In the largest cities the arrival of the railway was more disruptive. Companies needed land for stations and tracks and, in the 1840s, a British parliamentary inquiry recommended that they should be kept out of the historic heart of London. The result was a ring of terminals, among them Euston, King's Cross and Paddington, around the edge of the centre, and passengers had to complete their journeys by cab or on foot. Where lines did push inwards, they tended to cut through the poorest districts, because the land there was cheapest and its residents had the least influence. Tens of thousands of people lost their homes, and since they could rarely afford to move far, the surrounding streets became more crowded than before.

D  Stations became some of the most valuable pieces of urban real estate. Hotels, cafes, banks and offices clustered around them, and the grand station buildings, with their iron roofs and imposing facades, were designed to proclaim the confidence of the age. Railways also changed the way time itself was organised. Each town had traditionally set its clocks by the sun, which meant that noon in one place came minutes before noon in another. Timetables made nonsense of this, and railway companies began to use a single standard time along their lines, a practice that was gradually adopted by whole nations.

E  The most lasting effect, however, was on the pattern of residential life. Once season tickets and cheap workmen's fares became available, it was no longer necessary to live next door to one's job. Prosperous families moved out to new suburbs strung along the lines like beads on a thread, enjoying fresh air and larger gardens while the husband took the train to the office. Builders bought up farmland near stations, and the price of land rose steeply wherever a new halt was announced. The commuter, a figure who had barely existed a generation earlier, became a fixture of urban life. Newspapers and novelists of the period poked fun at the new suburban husband, who spent his mornings dashing for the early train and his evenings complaining about the price of his season ticket.

F  Underground railways extended the same logic. The first, opened in London in 1863, carried a large number of passengers on its opening day and was soon copied in other capitals. By making it possible to cross the centre quickly, the underground helped to relieve crowding in the central slums, although its builders gave little thought to where the displaced residents would go. Electric trams and trains, which arrived towards the end of the century, were cleaner and faster than steam, and pushed the edge of the built-up area further outward still.

G  In the twentieth century the car and the motorway threatened the railway's dominance, and many suburban lines closed. Yet the pattern laid down by the railway proved remarkably durable: the street plans, the commuter belts and even the commercial centres of today's cities still follow the old lines. More recently, planners in many countries have rediscovered the principle, and are encouraging dense housing, shops and offices around stations in the hope of persuading people to leave their cars at home. The railway age may be over, but its geography is far from finished.

passages.title: Is it fair? Animals and the sense of justice
paras: A  Few accusations sting like 'That's not fair!' Children as young as three will protest when a sibling is given a bigger slice of cake, and adults can nurse a grievance about an unequal pay rise for decades. For a long time, scientists assumed that this sensitivity to fairness was a purely human invention, a product of language, law and moral education. Over the past twenty years, however, a stream of experiments has claimed to find the roots of a sense of justice in animals, from monkeys to dogs. The claim has been widely reported, and widely welcomed. I believe the evidence is genuinely interesting, but that it has been oversold.

B  The best-known study was carried out by Dr Marta Oyelaran, who trained pairs of capuchin monkeys to hand a small token to a researcher in return for a slice of cucumber. The monkeys did this happily, until one of them watched its neighbour receive a grape, a far more desirable food, for exactly the same task. Many of the monkeys that were short-changed then refused to continue, and some hurled the cucumber back at the experimenter. Dr Oyelaran concluded that the animals had a dislike of unequal treatment. It is a vivid result, and it is easy to see why it caught the public imagination. Yet I am not persuaded by her interpretation. Prof Ingrid Halloran repeated the procedure but, on some trials, simply placed a grape in view without giving it to another monkey. The subjects protested almost as often. This suggests that they were reacting to the sight of a better reward, not to the sight of a rival being favoured, and disappointment is not the same thing as a sense of injustice.

C  The study of dogs, by Prof Samir Qureshi, seems to me more telling. Dogs were taught to give a paw on command and were then tested in pairs. When one dog was rewarded with a piece of sausage and its partner received nothing, the unrewarded animal stopped cooperating much sooner than a dog tested alone, with no partner and no rewards at all. The dog's behaviour changed because of what happened to another dog, and that is exactly the pattern a theory of fairness would predict. I would add one caution: the difference between the two conditions was modest, and more studies are needed before it can be called conclusive.

D  Chimpanzees, our closest relatives, ought to provide the most convincing evidence, but they have proved something of a disappointment. Dr Tomas Beaumont gave pairs of chimpanzees a version of the ultimatum game, in which one animal proposed how to divide a pile of food and the other could accept the split or reject it, leaving both with nothing. Human players typically turn down offers they regard as mean, even at a cost to themselves. The chimpanzees behaved like textbook economists: they accepted any offer, however small, provided it was more than zero. In a later experiment, though, animals that had worked together to pull in a heavy tray of food divided it far more evenly than those that had not. This finding seems to me more suggestive than any of the others, because it implies that fairness depends partly on whether the animals have cooperated.

E  Cooperation also lies behind the work of Dr Aiko Fenwick, who found that rats which had been helped by a partner were more willing to help that partner in return later on. This pattern, known as reciprocity, is often described as fairness, but the two are not the same. Reciprocity is a matter of repaying favours; fairness requires an abstract rule that applies to everyone, including oneself. Many people feel uncomfortable when they are paid more than a colleague for the same job. No animal has yet been shown to object when it receives more than its share, and until one does, I will remain unconvinced that the full human sense of fairness is shared.

F  Part of the trouble lies in the way the research is presented. Headlines announce that 'monkeys hate injustice' or 'dogs know right from wrong' long after the cautious language of the scientific papers has been forgotten. There is a danger in the opposite direction too. Some critics explain away every result as simple frustration, and I think that is a mistake. To dismiss all of this evidence in that way is as lazy as to over-read it. In both cases, we substitute a slogan for an experiment.

G  Why does it matter? If a sensitivity to unequal treatment is found in species as distant as monkeys and dogs, it probably evolved long ago, and for a good reason: groups whose members tolerate cheats are likely to fall apart. Fairness, on this view, is not a luxury of civilisation but a practical mechanism for keeping cooperation going. That possibility is worth taking seriously, and I would like to see more funding for careful studies of it, particularly with species that have never been tested.

H  My own conclusion is therefore a cautious one. Animals clearly show some of the building blocks of fairness: they notice what others receive, and they are reluctant to carry on cooperating when they are treated worse. What they have not been shown to possess is the complete package, in which the same rule is applied to oneself and to others. Until that evidence arrives, the most honest summary is that animals have the beginnings of a sense of fairness, but not the sense of fairness that we take for granted.
